```{r libraries, message = FALSE}
library(nlmixr2extra)
library(rxode2)
```

# What a clinical utility index is

A clinical utility index (CUI) puts the benefit and the risk of each
candidate regimen on one scale.  Every endpoint is turned into a
desirability between 0 and 1 (higher is better, so the probability of an
adverse event enters as one minus that probability), and the CUI is the
weighted mean of the desirabilities:

$$
\mathrm{CUI}(d) = \sum_k \tilde w_k \, u_k\!\left(EP_k(d)\right),
\qquad \tilde w_k = w_k \Big/ \sum_j w_j .
$$

Winzenborg, Soliman and Shebley (CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol 2021)
computed the endpoints from exposure-response models simulated over a dose
grid, and let patient preference weights choose the dose.  `cui()` does the
same from nlmixr2 fits and other fitted models, with parameter uncertainty,
so every recommendation comes with an interval and with how often each
regimen would be chosen.

# A simulated trial

A once-daily oral drug is studied at 50, 100, 200 and 400 mg for 12 weeks.
PK is one-compartment with weight on clearance.  Pain response and moderate
to severe hot flashes at week 12 both rise with the steady-state average
concentration (Cavg).

```{r simulate, message = FALSE}
truth <- function() {
  ini({
    tka <- log(1.2)
    tcl <- log(8)
    tv <- log(60)
    eta.cl ~ 0.09
    eta.v ~ 0.04
    prop.sd <- 0.15
  })
  model({
    ka <- exp(tka)
    cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl) * (WT / 70)^0.75
    v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
    cp <- linCmt()
    cp ~ prop(prop.sd)
  })
}

set.seed(2026)
n <- 60
subjects <- data.frame(ID = seq_len(4 * n), dose = rep(c(50, 100, 200, 400), each = n),
                       WT = round(rlnorm(4 * n, log(70), 0.2)))
# sparse PK at steady state on day 84
pkEvents <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(subjects)), function(i) {
  s <- subjects[i, ]
  rbind(data.frame(ID = s$ID, TIME = 0, AMT = s$dose, EVID = 1, II = 24, ADDL = 83, DV = NA,
                   WT = s$WT),
        data.frame(ID = s$ID, TIME = 24 * 83 + c(1, 3, 8, 24), AMT = 0, EVID = 0, II = 0,
                   ADDL = 0, DV = NA, WT = s$WT))
}))
sim <- as.data.frame(rxSolve(truth, events = pkEvents, keep = "WT"))
# the simulated observations (with residual error) fill DV of the PK records
pkData <- pkEvents
obs <- pkData$EVID == 0
pkData$DV[obs] <- sim$sim[match(paste(pkData$ID[obs], pkData$TIME[obs]),
                                paste(sim$id, sim$time))]
# true steady-state Cavg drives the week-12 outcomes
subjects$CAVG <- subjects$dose / (exp(log(8)) * (subjects$WT / 70)^0.75 *
                                    exp(rnorm(nrow(subjects), 0, 0.3)) * 24)
subjects$resp <- rbinom(nrow(subjects), 1, plogis(-1.2 + 1.6 * subjects$CAVG))
subjects$hf <- rbinom(nrow(subjects), 1, plogis(-3.0 + 1.4 * subjects$CAVG))
head(pkData)
```

# The models

The PK model is fit with nlmixr2; the two week-12 binary outcomes are
logistic regressions on Cavg.  Any fitted model that has
`cuiModelPredict()` methods can be an endpoint (`glm`, `lme4`, `glmmTMB`
and `brms` fits work out of the box).

```{r fitPK, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
pkModel <- function() {
  ini({
    tka <- log(1)
    tcl <- log(6)
    tv <- log(50)
    eta.cl ~ 0.1
    eta.v ~ 0.1
    prop.sd <- 0.2
  })
  model({
    ka <- exp(tka)
    cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl) * (WT / 70)^0.75
    v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
    cp <- linCmt()
    cp ~ prop(prop.sd)
  })
}
fitPK := nlmixr2(pkModel, pkData, "focei", control = foceiControl(print = 0))
fitPK$parFixed
```

```{r fitER, message = FALSE}
fitResp := glm(resp ~ CAVG, family = binomial, data = subjects)
fitHF := glm(hf ~ CAVG, family = binomial, data = subjects)
coef(fitResp)
coef(fitHF)
```

# Simulating the clinical utility index

Each endpoint names its model and how it is summarized for each regimen:

- pain response and hot flashes are the mean predicted probability of the
  logistic models (`cuiResponse()`), driven per virtual subject by the
  week-12 Cavg simulated from the PK fit (`cuiExposure()`);
- trough attainment is the fraction of subjects whose trough at week 12 is
  above 0.5 mg/L, straight from the PK model (`cuiThreshold()`).

Every regimen is simulated in the same target population, resampled from
the trial with its weights, and with the same virtual subjects, so the
comparison between regimens is not blurred by simulation noise.

```{r define}
endpoints <- list(
  cuiEndpoint(resp, fitResp, cuiResponse()),
  cuiEndpoint(trough, fitPK, cuiThreshold(cp > 0.5, time = 24 * 84)),
  cuiEndpoint(hotFlash, fitHF, cuiResponse(), direction = "lower")
)
doses <- seq(0, 600, by = 50)
regimens <- cuiRegimens(dose = doses, ii = 24, duration = 24 * 84, units = "mg",
                        label = as.character(doses))
exposure <- cuiExposure(fitPK, CAVG = cuiMean(cp, window = c(24 * 83, 24 * 84)))
population <- cuiPopulation(subjects, n = 400, covs = "WT", seed = 1)
```

Parameter uncertainty comes from each fit's covariance (`uncertainty =
"cov"`): structural thetas of the PK fit and the coefficients of the
logistic fits are drawn 200 times.  Draw 0 is the point estimate.

```{r cui, message = FALSE}
res := cui(endpoints, regimens, population, exposure = exposure,
           weights = c(resp = 2, trough = 1, hotFlash = 1),
           uncertainty = "cov", nDraw = 200, seed = 1, cacheDir = NA)
res
```

The CUI line with its band, and the endpoints behind it:

```{r plot-cui}
plot(res)
```

```{r plot-endpoints}
plot(res, "endpoints")
```

Pain response and trough attainment climb with dose while freedom from hot
flashes falls.  With these weights the benefit keeps paying for the risk,
but less and less: the CUI flattens from about 400 mg on and its bands
overlap there, so the highest dose wins only narrowly.  How often each dose
is the best across the parameter draws shows how soft that choice is:

```{r plot-selection}
plot(res, "selection")
```

# Patient preferences

The weights are the clinical judgment.  Re-weighting only recombines the
stored endpoint values, so it is instant -- nothing is simulated again.  For
a patient for whom hot flashes matter most, the CUI now has a clear peak at
a moderate dose:

```{r reweight}
hfAverse <- update(res, weights = c(resp = 1.5, trough = 0.5, hotFlash = 3.6))
plot(hfAverse, "endpoints")
```

Weights can also be set by endpoint group (`group` in `cuiEndpoint()`,
efficacy and safety by default): each group gets a weight and its endpoints
share it.

```{r groups}
w <- cuiGroupWeights(res, group = c(efficacy = 1, safety = 1),
                     within = c(resp = 3, trough = 1))
w
update(res, weights = w)$summary[, c("regimen", "est", "best")]
```

How far a preference has to move before the recommendation changes:

```{r sensitivity}
s <- cuiSensitivity(res)
s
plot(s)
```

# Restricting to available regimens

A recommendation for a patient has to be a dose that exists.  With the
eligible regimens restricted, the recommendation and the selection
frequencies are worked out among them only, and the plot marks them:

```{r eligible}
approved <- update(res, eligible = c("100", "300"))
plot(approved)
approved$summary[approved$summary$eligible, c("regimen", "est", "lower", "upper", "selFreq")]
```

# An interactive desk tool

`cuiApp()` opens the result in a Shiny app with one slider per endpoint
group and, under it, one per endpoint; `mode = "desk"` keeps the
recommendation to the eligible regimens.  `cuiAppExport()` writes a
deployable copy.

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
cuiApp(approved, mode = "desk",
       presets = list("Trial-like" = c(resp = 2, trough = 1, hotFlash = 1),
                      "Hot-flash averse" = c(resp = 1.5, trough = 0.5, hotFlash = 3.6)))
cuiAppExport(approved, "cuiDeskTool", mode = "desk")
```

# Other sources of uncertainty

- `uncertainty = cuiBootstrap(bootstrapFit(fitPK, nboot = 200,
  returnType = "fitList"))` uses bootstrap refits as the parameter draws.
- `mode = "trial"` keeps the parameters at their estimates and simulates
  finite trials of `nSub` subjects instead, so the bands describe
  trial-to-trial variation.

With a `seed`, `cui()` caches every draw (in `nlmixr2CuiCache_<md5>/` unless
`cacheDir` says otherwise), so a long simulation resumes where it stopped
and a larger `nDraw` only simulates the new draws.
